title: Rashmika Mandanna Launches Project Annapurna, Adopting 400 Families for Grocery Support
excerpt: The actor will cover grocery costs for 400 families at a time in three-month phases across eight South Indian locations, in an initiative she links to her Ranabaali character Jayamma.
body:
• Actor Rashmika Mandanna has launched Project Annapurna, adopting 400 families for grocery support across eight locations in South India.
  • Families will be supported in three-month phases, with the initiative set to continue over the next year.
  • Grocery kits reportedly include rice, whole wheat flour, pulses, cooking oil, ragi, spices and tea.
  • The eight locations are Hyderabad, Mahabubnagar, Anantapur, Bengaluru, Kochi, Chennai, Kodagu and Vijayawada, and the support is designed so families can redirect grocery money toward savings.

Actor Rashmika Mandanna has launched a year-long food support initiative, Project Annapurna, under which she has adopted 400 families and will cover their grocery needs in phases. She announced the programme in a video shared on social media, according to NDTV, explaining that she had previously kept her charitable work private but was speaking about this effort publicly in the hope that it might encourage others to help in their own way.

The announcement comes just ahead of the theatrical release of her film Ranabaali on October 16. Mandanna said the decision to go public was connected to Jayamma, the character she plays in the film, and to the similarities she sees between the character and herself.

How Project Annapurna Will Work

Under the initiative, 400 families at a time will receive grocery support for three months each, and the programme will continue in phases over the next year, Cinema Express reported. The coverage spans eight locations across South India: Hyderabad, Mahabubnagar and Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, Bengaluru and Kodagu in Karnataka, Kochi in Kerala, Chennai in Tamil Nadu, and Vijayawada.

The kits are practical rather than symbolic. They reportedly include staple items such as rice, whole wheat flour, pulses and cooking oil, along with ragi, spices and tea. Mandanna's stated logic is household budgeting: if a family's basic grocery bill is covered for a quarter, the money it would have spent on food can be saved instead and used to plan ahead.

"Even a small act of kindness can change a person's life, and it doesn't have to be big."

— Rashmika Mandanna, Actor

Mandanna said she had long done similar work quietly, with only her team aware of it, because she felt that was enough. She changed her approach this time, she explained, because a public example might prompt followers to start with something small themselves. She added that seeing the families' smiles made the sleepless nights, injuries and struggles of her working years feel worthwhile.

The Ranabaali Connection

The timing is closely tied to Ranabaali, a period drama directed by Rahul Sankrityan and set in 1870s South India against the backdrop of the Great Madras Famine of 1876–78. Vijay Deverakonda plays the titular warrior, while Mandanna plays Jayamma, his wife and companion in the struggle against colonial oppression. The film also features Arnold Vosloo as the British antagonist Sir Theodore Hector.

It is the third on-screen collaboration between Mandanna and Deverakonda, after Geetha Govindam and Dear Comrade, and their first together following their marriage. Mandanna has said that characters leave an imprint on the actors who play them, and that Jayamma's instinct to protect and provide for her people is one she recognises in herself. A famine-set story about food scarcity makes the choice of a grocery-support programme a direct extension of the film's subject.

What It Means and What Comes Next

For diaspora readers who send money home or fund community kitchens and food drives in their own cities, the structure is the transferable part: a fixed number of families, a defined three-month support window, and staple kits rather than one-off cash handouts. The same model scales down easily to a street, a village or an apartment block.

The first phase is now under way with the initial 400 families. How the programme rotates new families in over the remaining phases of the year, and whether other actors follow the public example Mandanna says she is trying to set, will determine whether Project Annapurna becomes a template or a one-release headline. Ranabaali opens in theatres on October 16.
